label: Marketing & customers
summary: Plan the marketing and then measure it: market size and demand, customer economics, campaign and channel performance, and the surveys and tests behind customer evidence.
start_steps: Size the market: Market size and Market share.
Check demand: Demand curve, Elasticity and Purchase intent.
Test customer economics: Unit economics, Cohort, RFM and CLV.
Measure the funnel and channels: Funnel, Campaign, Attribution, Channel economics and the channel tools.
Test a change: A/B test, Reliability (alpha), Chi-square and Power.
does_not: It does not connect to an ad platform or retrieve campaign data.
It does not recommend a budget, a bid or a segment.
It does not estimate a missing number or invent a customer.
guidance: Work down the page in the order a marketing plan is written. Size the market and test the demand first, then check whether a customer is worth acquiring, then measure the funnel and the digital channels that feed it, and finally test what you changed. Every figure is one you supply and confirm; the engine computes the arithmetic, runs its checks and states what it cannot tell you. It does not connect to an ad platform, estimate a missing number or recommend a budget.

tools.label: Market size (TAM, SAM, SOM)
tools.what: Size the whole market, the part you can serve and the part you can win from a population, an annual spend and two shares you declare.
tools.formula: TAM = customers x annual spend; SAM = TAM x serviceable share; SOM = SAM x obtainable share.
steps: Count the customers in the market you are describing, or use a population and a spend figure you can defend.
Multiply by the average annual spend for the total addressable market.
Apply the share of that market you can physically serve, then the share of that market you can win.
Check that each share is below one and that SOM is smaller than SAM, which is smaller than TAM.
common_mistakes: Presenting SOM as if it were the whole market.
Using a national population when the shop serves one barangay.
Mixing a monthly spend with an annual population figure.
Calling the shares evidence: they are assumptions unless you cite a source.

tools.label: Market share and penetration
tools.what: Read the share of a declared market, its change from a prior period, penetration against a population and the relative share against a named competitor.
tools.formula: Market share = firm sales / market sales; penetration = customers / target population; relative share = firm sales / largest competitor's sales.
steps: Decide the market boundary and keep it identical for every figure.
Enter the firm's sales and the whole market's sales for the same period and currency.
Add a prior period only if you have both sides of it, so the share change is comparable.
Add customers and population for penetration, and name the largest competitor for relative share.
common_mistakes: Widening or narrowing the market between the two periods.
Mixing a unit share with a revenue share.
Reading a share change as a trend when there are only two points.
Treating penetration as loyalty: a buyer may buy once and leave.

tools.label: Demand line and revenue-max price
tools.what: Fit a line to your price and quantity pairs and read the slope, the elasticity and the price that maximises revenue.
tools.formula: q = a + b p, fitted by least squares; elasticity at the mean = b x (mean price / mean quantity).
steps: Collect price-quantity pairs from the same market and period basis.
Enter the prices and the quantity demanded at each price.
Read the slope, the R-squared and the elasticity at the mean price.
If the slope is negative, read the revenue-maximising price on the fitted line.
common_mistakes: Treating the fitted line as an identified demand curve.
Mixing observations from different periods or markets.
Extrapolating far outside the observed price range.
Ignoring that price and quantity are jointly determined.

tools.label: Price elasticity of demand
tools.what: Measure the arc elasticity between two price-quantity observations and see what happens to revenue.
tools.formula: E = (% change in Q) / (% change in P), using the midpoint (arc) formula.
steps: Compute the change in quantity divided by the average quantity.
Compute the change in price divided by the average price.
Divide the first percentage change by the second.
Compare the absolute value with one and read the revenue change.
common_mistakes: Using the slope of the inverse demand curve instead of the percentage changes.
Calling a negative elasticity inelastic because the sign is negative.
Mixing percentages and decimals in the same calculation.
Using the point formula for a discrete change.

tools.label: Purchase intent
tools.what: Turn weighted survey answers into an expected buying rate, projected buyers and projected revenue.
tools.formula: Intent rate = (definitely x w1 + probably x w2 + maybe x w3 + never x w4) / respondents; projected buyers = population x intent rate.
steps: Enter how many respondents gave each answer.
Declare the weight each answer carries, or use the stated defaults.
Read the weighted intent rate.
If you declare the population and the price, read projected buyers and projected revenue.
common_mistakes: Treating stated intent as a sale.
Using weights without saying where they came from.
Projecting onto a population the sample does not represent.
Forgetting that the sample size limits the precision.

tools.label: Trend forecast
tools.what: Fit a trend to your own series and record the forecast periods and the range the result could fall in.
tools.need: a series in period order and the horizon
tools.formula: Fit y = a + bt to the series; the forecast extends the line and carries a prediction interval.
steps: Enter the series in order, one value per period.
Declare the horizon you want to forecast.
Read the trend, the forecast values and the interval.
Check the holdout error before trusting the extrapolation.
common_mistakes: Extrapolating far beyond the data without widening the interval.
Ignoring seasonality that a straight line cannot capture.
Reading a high R-squared as proof that the forecast is right.
Forecasting a series that changed regime.

tools.label: Unit economics
tools.what: The margin per customer, the cost to win one, its payback and lifetime value.
tools.formula: Contribution margin = price - variable cost; LTV = margin / churn; CAC payback = acquisition cost / margin.
steps: Enter the price and the variable cost per unit or customer.
Enter the acquisition cost and, if you know it, the churn rate.
Read the margin, the payback period and the LTV/CAC ratio.
Check that price and cost are for the same period.
common_mistakes: Using gross profit instead of contribution margin.
Entering churn as a percentage (5) instead of a decimal (0.05).
Comparing an undiscounted LTV with a discounted cost.
Treating a single churn rate as a retention curve.

tools.label: Multi-product break-even
tools.what: Find the sales mix at which several products together cover their fixed costs.
tools.formula: Weighted contribution = sum(mix weight x unit contribution); break-even units = fixed cost / weighted contribution.
steps: Compute each product's unit contribution.
Weight the contributions by the declared sales mix.
Divide fixed cost by the weighted contribution.
Split the break-even units back across the mix.
common_mistakes: Using a simple average instead of the mix-weighted contribution.
Letting the mix change while claiming one break-even point.
Ignoring capacity limits.

tools.label: Cohort retention
tools.what: Follow groups of customers who started together and read retention, churn and the average customer life.
tools.formula: Period retention = retained customers in that period / starting customers, pooled across cohorts; average lifetime = the sum of the period retention rates.
steps: Enter the number of customers in each cohort when it started.
Enter how many of each cohort were still buying in each later period.
Keep every cohort's row the same length; leave out a period a cohort has not reached.
Read the pooled retention curve, the churn and the average lifetime.
common_mistakes: Zero-filling a period the cohort has not reached yet.
Mixing revenue retention with customer retention.
Averaging cohort rates without weighting by cohort size.
Reading a lifetime as a forecast.

tools.label: RFM segmentation
tools.what: Score every customer on recency, frequency and monetary value, then see how many fall in each named segment and what the average scores are.
tools.formula: Rank customers inside the file, split the ranks into five equal-count bands, and score recency in reverse; the segment comes from the declared first-match rules on the three scores.
steps: Decide what counts as a purchase and over what window, then take recency, frequency and monetary value from the same records.
Give every customer a unique name so the rows can be checked back.
Read the segment sizes before the averages: a small Champions group and a large At-risk group call for different actions.
Say in your write-up that the bands are relative to this list, not an industry benchmark.
common_mistakes: Mixing a lifetime monetary value with a last-year frequency.
Treating the segment names as facts about customers rather than labels from a rule.
Forgetting that ties share a band, so the groups need not be equal.
Claiming the segments differ in behaviour without a test.

tools.label: Customer lifetime value
tools.what: Value a customer over a declared horizon with a churn and discount rate, and read the undiscounted value, the value per unit of acquisition cost and the payback period.
tools.formula: Value = sum over the horizon of margin x survival / (1 + discount rate)^period, where survival falls by the churn rate each period.
steps: Take the contribution margin the customer leaves in one period, not the revenue.
Declare the churn rate and the discount rate as decimals, and state the horizon.
Read the discounted value, then the undiscounted value, to see what time costs.
Add an acquisition cost only if you want the value ratio and the payback period.
common_mistakes: Using revenue instead of contribution margin.
Leaving the horizon unsaid, so the figure cannot be compared with another.
Forgetting that churn lowers later periods, not the first one.
Reading the value as a promise: it rests on a constant churn the method cannot test.

tools.label: Customer profitability by segment
tools.what: Enter revenue, direct cost and any allocated cost for each segment and read profit, margin, profit share and how few segments carry the profit.
tools.formula: Segment profit = revenue - direct cost - allocated cost; margin = profit / revenue; profit share = segment profit / total profit.
steps: Decide what counts as a segment and keep the definition identical across rows.
Enter revenue, direct cost and only the shared cost you can justify allocating.
Read the profitable and unprofitable counts before the shares.
Read the concentration count as a description of this snapshot, not a law.
common_mistakes: Allocating shared cost differently between two analyses and comparing the results.
Leaving fixed cost out and calling contribution accounting profit.
Treating a negative-profit segment as one to drop without checking the fixed cost it covers.
Comparing a monthly margin with an annual one.

tools.label: Campaign efficiency
tools.what: Enter impressions, clicks, conversions, spend and revenue and read the click-through, cost per click and per thousand impressions, cost per acquisition, return on ad spend and the break-even return.
tools.formula: Click-through rate = clicks / impressions; cost per click = spend / clicks; cost per acquisition = spend / conversions; return on ad spend = revenue / spend; break-even return = 1 / contribution margin rate.
steps: Agree the campaign, the period and what counts as a conversion before you start.
Enter impressions, clicks, conversions, spend and the revenue you attribute to the campaign.
Declare the contribution margin if you want the break-even return and the profit after media.
Compare the return on ad spend with the break-even figure, not with a rule of thumb.
common_mistakes: Comparing a return on ad spend with another campaign that defines a conversion differently.
Treating attributed revenue as the revenue the campaign caused.
Reading a high return as profit when the contribution margin is low.
Mixing a monthly spend with annual revenue.

tools.label: Attribution across channels
tools.what: Enter the credit each channel receives under first-click, last-click and linear rules and see how much the shares disagree.
tools.formula: Each channel's share under a rule = its credited conversions / the total credited conversions under that rule; the spread is the largest share minus the smallest.
steps: Choose the rules you will compare and keep the conversion definition fixed across them.
Enter each channel's credited conversions under first-click, last-click and linear.
Check that each rule allocates every conversion in full.
Read the largest spread as the channel whose apparent value depends most on the rule.
common_mistakes: Presenting one rule as the true value of a channel.
Comparing shares computed over different date ranges.
Treating attribution credit as proof the channel caused the sale.
Forgetting that branded search and direct traffic absorb credit under last-click.

tools.label: Channel economics
tools.what: Give each channel its spend, new customers, margin and churn and read acquisition cost, payback, lifetime value and the blended acquisition cost.
tools.formula: Acquisition cost = spend / new customers; payback = acquisition cost / contribution margin; lifetime value = contribution margin / churn rate; blended acquisition cost = total spend / total new customers.
steps: Assign each customer to the one channel that won them, and keep shared spend separate.
Enter each channel's spend, new customers, contribution margin per customer and period churn.
Read payback first: it says how long the cash takes to come back.
Read lifetime value and the ratio to acquisition cost second, against the same churn assumption.
common_mistakes: Pushing shared or brand spend into one channel.
Using revenue instead of contribution margin in the lifetime value.
Assuming churn stays constant for the whole life of the customer.
Comparing a blended acquisition cost with a single channel's cost.

tools.label: Email list health
tools.what: Read list growth, churn, open and click rates, click-to-open and revenue per subscriber from the counts you declare.
tools.formula: List end = start + new - unsubscribes - bounces; open rate = opens / sends; click rate = clicks / sends; revenue per subscriber = revenue / list end.
steps: Take the list size, the additions and the losses for the same period as the sends.
Keep opens and clicks for the same set of sends.
Read growth and churn together: a growing list can still be losing its most engaged readers.
Read revenue per subscriber beside the send counts, not on its own.
common_mistakes: Counting a machine open as a person reading the message.
Measuring churn against the closing list instead of the starting list.
Treating a high open rate as proof the message was read or liked.
Adding new subscribers without removing bounces and unsubscribes.

tools.label: Social reach and engagement
tools.what: Read engagement rate, frequency, cost per thousand impressions, cost per engagement and follower growth from the platform counts you declare.
tools.formula: Engagement rate = engagements / reach; frequency = impressions / reach; cost per thousand impressions = spend / impressions x 1,000; follower growth = net gain / starting followers.
steps: Decide one platform and one engagement definition, and keep them fixed.
Enter impressions, reach, engagements, the starting audience, the net follower change and any spend.
Read the engagement rate with the frequency beside it: the same person can be counted many times.
Compare only with the same platform, definition and period.
common_mistakes: Dividing engagements by impressions and calling it the same rate as reach.
Comparing engagement rates across platforms that count different actions.
Reading a follower gain as an audience that stayed.
Ignoring paid amplification behind an organic-looking post.

tools.label: Web traffic and conversion by channel
tools.what: Compare sessions, conversions, conversion rate and revenue per session across your acquisition channels, with organic-search click-through when you declare it.
tools.formula: Conversion rate = conversions / sessions; revenue per session = revenue / sessions; channel share = channel sessions / total sessions; blended rate pools every channel.
steps: List every acquisition channel, including direct and unattributed traffic.
Enter sessions, conversions and revenue for the same period and the same definition.
Read the conversion rate and revenue per session side by side: they answer different questions.
Add organic impressions and clicks only if you want the organic click-through.
common_mistakes: Leaving direct traffic out, which inflates every other channel's share.
Comparing channels measured with different session definitions or attribution windows.
Treating revenue per session as profit.
Reading a channel's conversion rate without its volume.

tools.label: Reach, frequency and rating points
tools.what: Enter the population and each vehicle's reach, insertions and cost and read rating points, cost per point, cost per thousand impressions and the combined reach under random duplication.
tools.formula: Rating points = reach share x average frequency x 100; gross impressions = reach x frequency; cost per point = cost / rating points; combined reach = 1 - the product of (1 - each reach share).
steps: Fix the target population and the period, then take each vehicle's reach, insertions and cost from the same plan.
Enter one row per vehicle and keep the names distinct.
Read the plan total in rating points, then the combined reach: points add up, reach does not.
Treat the combined reach as an upper bound, because real audiences overlap more than chance.
common_mistakes: Dividing cost by gross impressions when the question was cost per rating point.
Adding the vehicles' reach counts together and calling it the plan's reach.
Forgetting the population, so reach share cannot be computed.
Reading a rating point as a person rather than as one percent of the population seeing one insertion.

tools.label: Sales funnel and conversion
tools.what: Enter how many people reached each stage and read the conversion, the drop-off and the cost of winning a customer.
tools.formula: Stage conversion = count at the next stage / count at this stage; overall conversion = last count / first count.
steps: List the stages in the order a customer meets them.
Enter how many people reached each stage in the same period.
Read each stage's conversion, the overall conversion and the drop-off.
If you declare the spend, read the acquisition cost per customer.
common_mistakes: Reordering stages so a smaller count comes first.
Mixing periods between stages.
Counting the same customer twice in one stage.
Reading a conversion difference as statistical proof.

tools.label: A/B test result
tools.what: Enter the visitors and conversions for two variants and read the lift, the test result and the interval, plus how many visitors each arm needs for the effect you declare.
tools.formula: Absolute lift = rate B - rate A; pooled z = (rate B - rate A) / sqrt(p(1 - p)(1/nA + 1/nB)) with p the pooled rate; the interval for the difference uses unpooled standard errors.
steps: Decide the single metric and the smallest effect worth acting on before the test runs.
Let both arms run over the same window and split traffic at random.
Enter the visitors and conversions for each arm, then read the lift, the p-value and the interval.
Read the interval as well as the p-value: it shows the range of effects the sample cannot rule out.
common_mistakes: Stopping the test as soon as the p-value crosses the threshold.
Changing the metric after seeing the result.
Calling a significant result proof that the change caused the lift.
Running many variants or segments and reading the best one as the answer.

tools.label: Reliability (Cronbach's alpha)
tools.what: Check whether a set of survey items measures the same thing consistently, with the item and respondent counts stated.
tools.need: the items of your scale and the people who answered it
tools.formula: Cronbach's alpha = (k / (k - 1)) x (1 - sum of item variances / total variance), for k items.
steps: List the answers for every respondent to every survey item, keeping the same scale direction.
Check that higher scores mean the same thing on every item, reversing items where they do not.
Read alpha with the number of items and respondents beside it.
Report alpha as evidence about the instrument, not about the people who answered.
common_mistakes: Treating alpha as a measure of validity rather than internal consistency.
Reporting alpha without saying how many items and respondents it used.
Forgetting to reverse-code negatively worded items.
Assuming a high alpha means the scale measures one thing.

tools.label: Chi-square association
tools.what: Test whether two categorical variables are associated, with the expected-count checks.
tools.need: a two-way table of counts, and the categories in each direction
tools.formula: Chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected.
steps: Build the contingency table.
Check the expected counts.
Read the p-value and the effect size.
common_mistakes: Using chi-square with very small expected counts.
Reading causation into an association.
Ignoring the table's degrees of freedom.

tools.label: Power and sample size
tools.what: Record the sample size or power implied by a declared effect and alpha.
tools.need: the size of the effect you are looking for and the number of observations
tools.formula: Power depends on the effect size, alpha, sample size and variability.
steps: Declare the effect size you care about.
Choose alpha and the desired power.
Read the required sample size or the detectable effect.
common_mistakes: Choosing the effect size after seeing the data.
Confusing power with the p-value.
Ignoring attrition and clustering.

tiles.label: Customer economics and retention
tiles.what: What a customer is worth and whether they come back: unit economics, unit and multi-product break-even, cohort retention, the recency-frequency-monetary view of the customer base, customer lifetime value and profit by customer.
tiles.need: The transaction or subscription history you hold, the window you are measuring over, and the costs that attach to serving a customer.

tools.label: Unit economics
tools.what: The margin per customer, the cost to win one, its payback and lifetime value.
tools.formula: Contribution margin = price - variable cost; LTV = margin / churn; CAC payback = acquisition cost / margin.
steps: Enter the price and the variable cost per unit or customer.
Enter the acquisition cost and, if you know it, the churn rate.
Read the margin, the payback period and the LTV/CAC ratio.
Check that price and cost are for the same period.
common_mistakes: Using gross profit instead of contribution margin.
Entering churn as a percentage (5) instead of a decimal (0.05).
Comparing an undiscounted LTV with a discounted cost.
Treating a single churn rate as a retention curve.

tools.label: Multi-product break-even
tools.what: Find the sales mix at which several products together cover their fixed costs.
tools.formula: Weighted contribution = sum(mix weight x unit contribution); break-even units = fixed cost / weighted contribution.
steps: Compute each product's unit contribution.
Weight the contributions by the declared sales mix.
Divide fixed cost by the weighted contribution.
Split the break-even units back across the mix.
common_mistakes: Using a simple average instead of the mix-weighted contribution.
Letting the mix change while claiming one break-even point.
Ignoring capacity limits.

tools.label: Cohort retention
tools.what: Follow groups of customers who started together and read retention, churn and the average customer life.
tools.formula: Period retention = retained customers in that period / starting customers, pooled across cohorts; average lifetime = the sum of the period retention rates.
steps: Enter the number of customers in each cohort when it started.
Enter how many of each cohort were still buying in each later period.
Keep every cohort's row the same length; leave out a period a cohort has not reached.
Read the pooled retention curve, the churn and the average lifetime.
common_mistakes: Zero-filling a period the cohort has not reached yet.
Mixing revenue retention with customer retention.
Averaging cohort rates without weighting by cohort size.
Reading a lifetime as a forecast.

tools.label: RFM segmentation
tools.what: Score every customer on recency, frequency and monetary value, then see how many fall in each named segment and what the average scores are.
tools.formula: Rank customers inside the file, split the ranks into five equal-count bands, and score recency in reverse; the segment comes from the declared first-match rules on the three scores.
steps: Decide what counts as a purchase and over what window, then take recency, frequency and monetary value from the same records.
Give every customer a unique name so the rows can be checked back.
Read the segment sizes before the averages: a small Champions group and a large At-risk group call for different actions.
Say in your write-up that the bands are relative to this list, not an industry benchmark.
common_mistakes: Mixing a lifetime monetary value with a last-year frequency.
Treating the segment names as facts about customers rather than labels from a rule.
Forgetting that ties share a band, so the groups need not be equal.
Claiming the segments differ in behaviour without a test.

tools.label: Customer lifetime value
tools.what: Value a customer over a declared horizon with a churn and discount rate, and read the undiscounted value, the value per unit of acquisition cost and the payback period.
tools.formula: Value = sum over the horizon of margin x survival / (1 + discount rate)^period, where survival falls by the churn rate each period.
steps: Take the contribution margin the customer leaves in one period, not the revenue.
Declare the churn rate and the discount rate as decimals, and state the horizon.
Read the discounted value, then the undiscounted value, to see what time costs.
Add an acquisition cost only if you want the value ratio and the payback period.
common_mistakes: Using revenue instead of contribution margin.
Leaving the horizon unsaid, so the figure cannot be compared with another.
Forgetting that churn lowers later periods, not the first one.
Reading the value as a promise: it rests on a constant churn the method cannot test.

tools.label: Customer profitability by segment
tools.what: Enter revenue, direct cost and any allocated cost for each segment and read profit, margin, profit share and how few segments carry the profit.
tools.formula: Segment profit = revenue - direct cost - allocated cost; margin = profit / revenue; profit share = segment profit / total profit.
steps: Decide what counts as a segment and keep the definition identical across rows.
Enter revenue, direct cost and only the shared cost you can justify allocating.
Read the profitable and unprofitable counts before the shares.
Read the concentration count as a description of this snapshot, not a law.
common_mistakes: Allocating shared cost differently between two analyses and comparing the results.
Leaving fixed cost out and calling contribution accounting profit.
Treating a negative-profit segment as one to drop without checking the fixed cost it covers.
Comparing a monthly margin with an annual one.

tools.label: Campaign efficiency
tools.what: Enter impressions, clicks, conversions, spend and revenue and read the click-through, cost per click and per thousand impressions, cost per acquisition, return on ad spend and the break-even return.
tools.formula: Click-through rate = clicks / impressions; cost per click = spend / clicks; cost per acquisition = spend / conversions; return on ad spend = revenue / spend; break-even return = 1 / contribution margin rate.
steps: Agree the campaign, the period and what counts as a conversion before you start.
Enter impressions, clicks, conversions, spend and the revenue you attribute to the campaign.
Declare the contribution margin if you want the break-even return and the profit after media.
Compare the return on ad spend with the break-even figure, not with a rule of thumb.
common_mistakes: Comparing a return on ad spend with another campaign that defines a conversion differently.
Treating attributed revenue as the revenue the campaign caused.
Reading a high return as profit when the contribution margin is low.
Mixing a monthly spend with annual revenue.

tools.label: Attribution across channels
tools.what: Enter the credit each channel receives under first-click, last-click and linear rules and see how much the shares disagree.
tools.formula: Each channel's share under a rule = its credited conversions / the total credited conversions under that rule; the spread is the largest share minus the smallest.
steps: Choose the rules you will compare and keep the conversion definition fixed across them.
Enter each channel's credited conversions under first-click, last-click and linear.
Check that each rule allocates every conversion in full.
Read the largest spread as the channel whose apparent value depends most on the rule.
common_mistakes: Presenting one rule as the true value of a channel.
Comparing shares computed over different date ranges.
Treating attribution credit as proof the channel caused the sale.
Forgetting that branded search and direct traffic absorb credit under last-click.

tools.label: Channel economics
tools.what: Give each channel its spend, new customers, margin and churn and read acquisition cost, payback, lifetime value and the blended acquisition cost.
tools.formula: Acquisition cost = spend / new customers; payback = acquisition cost / contribution margin; lifetime value = contribution margin / churn rate; blended acquisition cost = total spend / total new customers.
steps: Assign each customer to the one channel that won them, and keep shared spend separate.
Enter each channel's spend, new customers, contribution margin per customer and period churn.
Read payback first: it says how long the cash takes to come back.
Read lifetime value and the ratio to acquisition cost second, against the same churn assumption.
common_mistakes: Pushing shared or brand spend into one channel.
Using revenue instead of contribution margin in the lifetime value.
Assuming churn stays constant for the whole life of the customer.
Comparing a blended acquisition cost with a single channel's cost.

tools.label: Email list health
tools.what: Read list growth, churn, open and click rates, click-to-open and revenue per subscriber from the counts you declare.
tools.formula: List end = start + new - unsubscribes - bounces; open rate = opens / sends; click rate = clicks / sends; revenue per subscriber = revenue / list end.
steps: Take the list size, the additions and the losses for the same period as the sends.
Keep opens and clicks for the same set of sends.
Read growth and churn together: a growing list can still be losing its most engaged readers.
Read revenue per subscriber beside the send counts, not on its own.
common_mistakes: Counting a machine open as a person reading the message.
Measuring churn against the closing list instead of the starting list.
Treating a high open rate as proof the message was read or liked.
Adding new subscribers without removing bounces and unsubscribes.

tools.label: Social reach and engagement
tools.what: Read engagement rate, frequency, cost per thousand impressions, cost per engagement and follower growth from the platform counts you declare.
tools.formula: Engagement rate = engagements / reach; frequency = impressions / reach; cost per thousand impressions = spend / impressions x 1,000; follower growth = net gain / starting followers.
steps: Decide one platform and one engagement definition, and keep them fixed.
Enter impressions, reach, engagements, the starting audience, the net follower change and any spend.
Read the engagement rate with the frequency beside it: the same person can be counted many times.
Compare only with the same platform, definition and period.
common_mistakes: Dividing engagements by impressions and calling it the same rate as reach.
Comparing engagement rates across platforms that count different actions.
Reading a follower gain as an audience that stayed.
Ignoring paid amplification behind an organic-looking post.

tools.label: Web traffic and conversion by channel
tools.what: Compare sessions, conversions, conversion rate and revenue per session across your acquisition channels, with organic-search click-through when you declare it.
tools.formula: Conversion rate = conversions / sessions; revenue per session = revenue / sessions; channel share = channel sessions / total sessions; blended rate pools every channel.
steps: List every acquisition channel, including direct and unattributed traffic.
Enter sessions, conversions and revenue for the same period and the same definition.
Read the conversion rate and revenue per session side by side: they answer different questions.
Add organic impressions and clicks only if you want the organic click-through.
common_mistakes: Leaving direct traffic out, which inflates every other channel's share.
Comparing channels measured with different session definitions or attribution windows.
Treating revenue per session as profit.
Reading a channel's conversion rate without its volume.

tools.label: Reach, frequency and rating points
tools.what: Enter the population and each vehicle's reach, insertions and cost and read rating points, cost per point, cost per thousand impressions and the combined reach under random duplication.
tools.formula: Rating points = reach share x average frequency x 100; gross impressions = reach x frequency; cost per point = cost / rating points; combined reach = 1 - the product of (1 - each reach share).
steps: Fix the target population and the period, then take each vehicle's reach, insertions and cost from the same plan.
Enter one row per vehicle and keep the names distinct.
Read the plan total in rating points, then the combined reach: points add up, reach does not.
Treat the combined reach as an upper bound, because real audiences overlap more than chance.
common_mistakes: Dividing cost by gross impressions when the question was cost per rating point.
Adding the vehicles' reach counts together and calling it the plan's reach.
Forgetting the population, so reach share cannot be computed.
Reading a rating point as a person rather than as one percent of the population seeing one insertion.

tools.label: Sales funnel and conversion
tools.what: Enter how many people reached each stage and read the conversion, the drop-off and the cost of winning a customer.
tools.formula: Stage conversion = count at the next stage / count at this stage; overall conversion = last count / first count.
steps: List the stages in the order a customer meets them.
Enter how many people reached each stage in the same period.
Read each stage's conversion, the overall conversion and the drop-off.
If you declare the spend, read the acquisition cost per customer.
common_mistakes: Reordering stages so a smaller count comes first.
Mixing periods between stages.
Counting the same customer twice in one stage.
Reading a conversion difference as statistical proof.

tools.label: A/B test result
tools.what: Enter the visitors and conversions for two variants and read the lift, the test result and the interval, plus how many visitors each arm needs for the effect you declare.
tools.formula: Absolute lift = rate B - rate A; pooled z = (rate B - rate A) / sqrt(p(1 - p)(1/nA + 1/nB)) with p the pooled rate; the interval for the difference uses unpooled standard errors.
steps: Decide the single metric and the smallest effect worth acting on before the test runs.
Let both arms run over the same window and split traffic at random.
Enter the visitors and conversions for each arm, then read the lift, the p-value and the interval.
Read the interval as well as the p-value: it shows the range of effects the sample cannot rule out.
common_mistakes: Stopping the test as soon as the p-value crosses the threshold.
Changing the metric after seeing the result.
Calling a significant result proof that the change caused the lift.
Running many variants or segments and reading the best one as the answer.

tools.label: Reliability (Cronbach's alpha)
tools.what: Check whether a set of survey items measures the same thing consistently, with the item and respondent counts stated.
tools.need: the items of your scale and the people who answered it
tools.formula: Cronbach's alpha = (k / (k - 1)) x (1 - sum of item variances / total variance), for k items.
steps: List the answers for every respondent to every survey item, keeping the same scale direction.
Check that higher scores mean the same thing on every item, reversing items where they do not.
Read alpha with the number of items and respondents beside it.
Report alpha as evidence about the instrument, not about the people who answered.
common_mistakes: Treating alpha as a measure of validity rather than internal consistency.
Reporting alpha without saying how many items and respondents it used.
Forgetting to reverse-code negatively worded items.
Assuming a high alpha means the scale measures one thing.

tools.label: Chi-square association
tools.what: Test whether two categorical variables are associated, with the expected-count checks.
tools.need: a two-way table of counts, and the categories in each direction
tools.formula: Chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected.
steps: Build the contingency table.
Check the expected counts.
Read the p-value and the effect size.
common_mistakes: Using chi-square with very small expected counts.
Reading causation into an association.
Ignoring the table's degrees of freedom.

tools.label: Power and sample size
tools.what: Record the sample size or power implied by a declared effect and alpha.
tools.need: the size of the effect you are looking for and the number of observations
tools.formula: Power depends on the effect size, alpha, sample size and variability.
steps: Declare the effect size you care about.
Choose alpha and the desired power.
Read the required sample size or the detectable effect.
common_mistakes: Choosing the effect size after seeing the data.
Confusing power with the p-value.
Ignoring attrition and clustering.

glossary.definition: Total addressable market is all the spending in the market you describe; the serviceable available market is the part you can reach; the serviceable obtainable market is the part you can realistically win.
How quantity demanded changes as price changes; its slope and the elasticity at the mean are what the demand tool reports.
The percentage change in quantity demanded for a one-percent change in price; above one in absolute value is elastic, below one is inelastic.
What survey respondents say they will buy, weighted into an expected buying rate; a statement of intent, not a record of purchases.
Customer acquisition cost: what you spend, on average, to win one customer.
Customer lifetime value: the contribution a customer brings over their life; here, margin divided by the declared churn rate.
The share of customers who stop buying each period, entered as a decimal (5% is 0.05).
The share of a cohort still buying in a later period; its complement is churn.
A group of customers who started in the same period, followed together over later periods.
Price minus variable cost per unit: what each sale leaves towards fixed costs and profit.
The ordered stages a customer passes through, from first contact to purchase, with the count at each stage.
The share of the people at one stage who reach the next stage, or the share of visitors who complete the desired action.
The share of free trials that become paying customers, measured over a declared window.
Click-through rate: clicks divided by impressions.
Cost per click: advertising spend divided by clicks.
Cost per thousand impressions: spend divided by impressions, multiplied by 1,000.
Cost per acquisition: spend divided by the number of customers or actions won.
Return on ad spend: revenue attributed to the campaign divided by the spend.
Advertising cost of sales: spend divided by revenue, the inverse of ROAS, expressed as a percentage.
The ROAS at which campaign revenue exactly covers spend after the contribution margin: 1 / contribution margin ratio.
The rule that decides which touchpoint receives credit for a conversion; first-click, last-click, linear and position-based rules give different answers.
The conversions that would not have happened without the campaign; a causal question that attribution credit alone cannot answer.
The tagging convention (source, medium, campaign, content, term) that lets analytics group visits by where they came from.
Search engine optimisation: earning unpaid search traffic by making pages relevant and technically sound.
Search engine marketing: paid search advertising, usually charged per click.
Conversion-rate optimisation: changing a page or journey and testing whether the completion rate really improved.
A controlled comparison of two versions, where the difference in outcomes is tested against the range chance alone could produce.
The chance a test detects a real effect of a declared size; it sets the sample you need before you start.
Marketing-qualified lead and sales-qualified lead: two declared stages a lead passes before it becomes an opportunity.
How the budget is divided across channels, and the evidence for what each channel returns.
Recency, frequency and monetary value: three transaction-based measures used to group customers by buying behaviour.
Classifies product attributes by how their presence or absence affects satisfaction, from must-be to attractive.
A service-quality instrument that compares customer expectations with perceptions across declared dimensions.
A one-to-five band given by ranking the customers in your own file into five equal-count groups; the top band is five, and recency is ranked in reverse.
A label taken from a declared grid of recency, frequency and monetary scores, such as Champions or At risk; the label describes buying behaviour in one snapshot.
The number of people who see a vehicle at least once in the period, counted once each however many times they see it.
Reach divided by the declared target population, expressed as a decimal (45% is 0.45).
The average number of times a reached person sees the message; for a plan it is gross impressions divided by combined reach.
Reach multiplied by average frequency: a count of exposures, not of people.
Gross rating points: reach share times average frequency times one hundred. Points add up across vehicles; people do not.
Cost per rating point: cost divided by gross rating points, the price of one percent of the population seeing one insertion.
The combined number of different people a set of vehicles reaches; estimated here by the random-duplication formula, so it is an upper bound.
The firm's sales divided by the total sales of the declared market, over the same period and in the same currency.
The share of the declared target population that buys; it counts buyers once, however often they buy.
The firm's sales divided by the largest declared competitor's sales; above one means the firm is the leader.
The margin a customer is expected to leave over a declared horizon, discounted to today and reduced each period by churn.
The per-period rate used to bring a future amount back to today; a higher rate makes future margin worth less.
How few segments produce a declared share of the total profit, read from the segments ranked by profit.
